Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra with
Killing form $B$ ([[def-killing-form-of-a-finite-dimensional-lie-algebra]]). A
**compact real form** of $\mathfrak g$ is a real form $\mathfrak g_0$ of
$\mathfrak g$ ([[def-real-form-of-a-complex-lie-algebra]]) whose Killing form
$B_{\mathfrak g_0}=B|_{\mathfrak g_0\times\mathfrak g_0}$ is **negative
definite**, that is $B(X,X)<0$ for every nonzero $X\in\mathfrak g_0$ and
$B(X,X)=0$ if and only if $X=0$. A real Lie algebra is called **compact** when
its Killing form is negative definite; under this terminology the compact real
forms are exactly the real forms that are compact as real Lie algebras. The
existence and conjugacy of compact real forms are the content of
[[thm-existence-of-a-compact-real-form]] and
[[thm-conjugacy-of-compact-real-forms]].

Use [[def-loop-algebra-of-a-simple-lie-algebra]]. Fix the positive-real rescaling $B$ of the Killing form whose induced form on the real finite-root span makes every long root have square $2$. The Killing form is nondegenerate, invariant and symmetric by [[lem-finite-lie-engel-trace-criterion-and-killing-nondegeneracy]], and its restriction gives a positive definite real root form by [[lem-finite-semisimple-cartan-root-and-string-structure]], so this rescaling exists. In particular $B([x,y],z)=B(x,[y,z])$.

For $f=\sum_m a_mt^m$ put $f'=\sum_m ma_mt^{m-1}$ and $\operatorname{Res}(f\,dt)=a_{-1}$. Define the residue bilinear form by
$$\omega(x\otimes f,y\otimes q)=B(x,y)\operatorname{Res}(f'q\,dt).$$
The formula is balanced and complex bilinear, so extends uniquely to the tensor product. In particular,
$$\omega(x_m,y_n)=m\delta_{m,-n}B(x,y).$$
The Kronecker symbol is one when $m=-n$ and zero otherwise. This form is in fact an alternating Lie-algebra two-cocycle. For Laurent polynomials $f,q$, the residue of $(fq)'$ is zero, so $\operatorname{Res}(f'q\,dt)=-\operatorname{Res}(fq'\,dt)$; symmetry of $B$ gives skew-symmetry, and in characteristic zero also $\omega(a,a)=0$. For pure tensors $x\otimes f,y\otimes q,z\otimes h$, invariance and symmetry of $B$ make the three factors $B([x,y],z)$, $B([y,z],x)$, and $B([z,x],y)$ equal. The cyclic cocycle sum is therefore that common factor times
$$\operatorname{Res}\bigl(((fq)'h+(qh)'f+(hf)'q)\,dt\bigr)=2\operatorname{Res}((fqh)'\,dt)=0.$$
Trilinearity extends the identity to all loop-algebra elements. Thus the terminology “two-cocycle” records a proved property of the defined form, not merely an intended later use.

For any long root $\alpha$, opposite root vectors normalized by $[e_\alpha,f_\alpha]=\alpha^\vee$ satisfy
$$B(e_\alpha,f_\alpha)=\frac{2}{(\alpha,\alpha)}=1.$$
The equality follows by pairing $[e_\alpha,f_\alpha]$ with the Cartan and using invariance. A later result identifies the highest root and proves that it is long; no highest-root existence claim is used here.

Let $\mathfrak g$ be finite-dimensional and let $B$ be a nondegenerate,
symmetric, invariant bilinear form on it. If
$x_1,\ldots,x_n$ is a basis and $x^1,\ldots,x^n$ is its $B$-dual basis, the
**Casimir element relative to $B$** is

$$\Omega_B=\sum_{i=1}^n x_i x^i\in U(\mathfrak g).$$

On a representation $\rho:\mathfrak g\to\mathfrak{gl}(V)$, its **Casimir
operator** is

$$\rho(\Omega_B)=\sum_{i=1}^n\rho(x_i)\rho(x^i).$$

The empty sums give zero when $\mathfrak g=0$. Nondegeneracy is exactly what
identifies $\mathfrak g$ with its dual and supplies the dual basis.
Independence of the chosen basis and commutation with the action are proved in
the next lemma.

Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional complex simple Lie algebra, let $B$ be the invariant form normalized so long roots have square $2$, and let $\mathfrak k$ be a compact real form. The adjoint action of the Casimir $\Omega_B$ from [[def-casimir-operator-relative-to-an-invariant-form]] is a unique positive scalar $\gamma_B$ times the identity.

derivations.claim: Set $Q=-B|_{\mathfrak k}$. By [F1] and [F2], $Q$ is positive definite. Choose a $Q$-orthonormal basis $(X_i)$ of $\mathfrak k$. Since $B=-Q$ on $\mathfrak k$, its $B$-dual basis is $(-X_i)$, and [F3] gives $\Omega_B=-\sum_iX_i^2$.

Applying the adjoint representation to step 1.1 gives $\operatorname{ad}(\Omega_B)=-\sum_i\operatorname{ad}(X_i)^2=\gamma_B I$ by [F4]. The definition $h^\vee=\gamma_B/2$ therefore yields $-\sum_i\operatorname{ad}(X_i)^2=2h^\vee I$, as stated.

$$K_{\mathfrak g}(x,y)=\operatorname{tr}_{\mathfrak g}(\operatorname{ad}_x\operatorname{ad}_y).$$

space $\mathfrak g$ itself. In particular, if $\mathfrak g=0$ or if
$\mathfrak g$ is abelian, then every adjoint operator is zero and
$K_{\mathfrak g}=0$. Symmetry and invariance will follow from the general
trace-form calculation rather than being included in the definition.

linear. Choose any ordered basis $\mathcal B$ of $V$ and define the **trace of
the endomorphism $T$** by

$$\operatorname{tr}(T):=\operatorname{tr}([T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal B}).$$

two ordered bases are similar, and similar matrices have equal trace. When
$V$ is the zero space, the empty basis gives trace $0$.

For a square matrix $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(F)$, its **trace** is the sum of its

$$\operatorname{tr}(A):=\sum_{i\in n}a_{ii}.$$

derivations.claim: Fix one finite basis $x_1,\ldots,x_N$ and its $B$-dual basis $x^1,\ldots,x^N$, so $B(x_i,x^j)=\delta_i^j$. If $T x_i=\sum_j t_{ji}x_j$, then $B(Tx_i,x^i)=t_{ii}$ by duality. Therefore [F3] gives $\operatorname{tr}(T)=\sum_iB(Tx_i,x^i)$. All choices here are finite and $B$ is nondegenerate by [F1].

For arbitrary $x,y\in\mathfrak g$, [F2], symmetry and invariance give
$$B(Cx,y)=\sum_iB([x_i,[x^i,x]],y)=\sum_iB([x^i,x],[y,x_i])=\sum_iB([x,[y,x_i]],x^i).$$
Indeed the first conversion uses $B([a,b],c)=B(b,[c,a])$ with $a=x_i$, and the second uses the same identity with $a=x$, followed by symmetry. Step 1.1 identifies the final sum with $\operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{ad}(x)\operatorname{ad}(y))=K_{\mathfrak g}(x,y)$. Thus $B(Cx,y)=K_{\mathfrak g}(x,y)$, with no compact real form or spectral assertion.

By [F1], $K_{\mathfrak g}(x,y)=c^{-1}B(x,y)$. Step 1.2 implies $B(Cx-c^{-1}x,y)=0$ for every $y$, so nondegeneracy yields $Cx=c^{-1}x$ for every $x$. Hence $C=\gamma_B I$ with $\gamma_B=c^{-1}>0$. The scalar is unique because $\mathfrak g\ne0$. Its half $h^\vee=\gamma_B/2$ is therefore well defined and positive without a compact-form existence theorem or a choice axiom.

If a compact real form $\mathfrak k$ is supplied, [F1] and [F4] make $Q=-B|_{\mathfrak k}$ positive definite. Take a finite $Q$-orthonormal real basis $(X_i)$ by [F4]; it is also a complex basis of $\mathfrak g$ because $\mathfrak k$ is a real form. Its $B$-dual basis is $(-X_i)$, since $B(X_i,-X_j)=\delta_{ij}$. Thus [F2] gives $C=-\sum_i\operatorname{ad}(X_i)^2$, and step 2.1 identifies this with $2h^\vee I$. This proves the conditional compact-basis formula without constructing a compact real form or inferring its existence from its definition.

Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional complex simple Lie algebra as in [[def-loop-algebra-of-a-simple-lie-algebra]], with normalized invariant form $B$ from [[def-untwisted-affine-central-extension]]. Let $\rho$ be a restricted affine-current module of level $k$ as in [[def-positive-energy-affine-module]], and assume $k+h^\vee\ne0$ for the number in [[def-dual-coxeter-number-for-normalized-form]]. Choose any $B$-dual bases $(x_a)$ and $(x^a)$ of $\mathfrak g$. Write $J_x(n)=\rho(x\otimes t^n)$.

For modes, define
$$:J_{x_a}(r)J_{x^a}(s):=\begin{cases}J_{x_a}(r)J_{x^a}(s),&r<0,\\J_{x^a}(s)J_{x_a}(r),&r\ge0.\end{cases}$$
The **Sugawara mode** of index $m\in\mathbb Z$ is
$$L_m=\frac{1}{2(k+h^\vee)}\sum_a\sum_{r\in\mathbb Z}:J_{x_a}(r)J_{x^a}(m-r):.$$
For the compact real form of [[def-compact-real-form-of-a-complex-semisimple-lie-algebra]], put $Q=-B|_{\mathfrak k}$; it is positive by the normalized form in [[def-residue-two-cocycle-on-a-loop-algebra]]. If $(X_i)$ is $Q$-orthonormal, then $( -X_i)$ is its $B$-dual, so the same formula reads
$$L_m=-\frac{1}{2(k+h^\vee)}\sum_i\sum_{r\in\mathbb Z}:J_{X_i}(r)J_{X_i}(m-r):.$$
By [[lem-sugawara-quadratic-modes-well-defined]], the mode sum is locally finite on every vector and independent of the chosen dual bases. At the **critical level** $k=-h^\vee$ the scalar denominator is zero and this normalized formula is not defined; no operator is asserted there.

For a finite-dimensional complex simple Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$ as in [[def-loop-algebra-of-a-simple-lie-algebra]], use the invariant form $B$ normalized by long roots of square $2$ in [[def-residue-two-cocycle-on-a-loop-algebra]]. By [[lem-adjoint-casimir-is-positive-scalar]], the Casimir $\Omega_B$ from [[def-casimir-operator-relative-to-an-invariant-form]] acts in the adjoint representation as $\gamma_B I$ for a unique positive real scalar $\gamma_B$. Define the **dual Coxeter number** by $h^\vee=\gamma_B/2$. Thus, for a $Q=-B|_{\mathfrak k}$-orthonormal basis of a compact real form from [[def-compact-real-form-of-a-complex-semisimple-lie-algebra]], $-\sum_i\operatorname{ad}(X_i)^2=2h^\vee I$; this is the normalization used in the affine central term and every Sugawara denominator below.

The **untwisted central extension** is the vector space $\overline{L\mathfrak g}=L\mathfrak g\oplus\mathbb Cc$, with $c$ a new nonzero basis vector, and bracket
$$[u+ac,v+bc]=[u,v]_{L\mathfrak g}+\omega(u,v)c.$$
Here $L\mathfrak g$ is [[def-loop-algebra-of-a-simple-lie-algebra]], while $B$ and $\omega$ are exactly the normalized invariant form and residue cocycle of [[def-residue-two-cocycle-on-a-loop-algebra]]. Their alternatingness and cocycle identity are proved in [[lem-the-loop-residue-form-is-alternating]] and [[lem-the-loop-residue-form-satisfies-the-lie-two-cocycle-identity]]. Thus $c$ is central, and for $x_m=x\otimes t^m$,
$$[x_m,y_n]=[x,y]_{m+n}+m\delta_{m,-n}B(x,y)c.$$
The bracket is bilinear and alternating by the first cited lemma. Its Jacobi sum has loop component zero by loop Jacobi and central component $\omega([u,v],w)+\omega([v,w],u)+\omega([w,u],v)=0$ by the second lemma. Central inputs give zero directly. Hence this defines a Lie algebra. The projection to $L\mathfrak g$ is a surjective Lie homomorphism with kernel $\mathbb Cc$. The vector-space inclusion of the loop algebra need not preserve its bracket. No universal property of this extension is asserted.

Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional complex simple Lie algebra with the invariant form used in [[def-untwisted-affine-central-extension]]. A representation $\rho$ of the loop central extension $\overline{L\mathfrak g}$ is a **restricted affine-current module of level $k\in\mathbb C$** if the central generator acts as $k\operatorname{id}$ and, for every vector $v$ and current $x\in\mathfrak g$, there is an integer $N(v,x)$ such that $\rho(x\otimes t^n)v=0$ for all $n\ge N(v,x)$.

The algebra in this definition is the central extension only; it does not contain the degree derivation. Restrictedness is a mode-truncation condition and does not itself supply an energy grading. A compatible positive-energy grading is extra structure on this current algebra.

Let $\mathfrak k$ be the compact real form of the complex simple algebra underlying [[def-positive-energy-affine-module]]. A **positive-energy unitary module** consists of a complex inner-product space (not assumed complete) with positive-definite inner product
$$H=\bigoplus_{r\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}}H_r,$$
where the displayed direct sum is orthogonal. Each $H_r$ is finite-dimensional and $H_0\ne0$. The representation of the restricted affine-current algebra has central level an integer $k\ge0$, satisfies $X(n)H_r\subseteq H_{r-n}$ for every $X\in\mathfrak k$ (with $H_s=0$ for $s<0$), and satisfies $X(n)^*=-X(-n)$. In particular zero modes are skew-adjoint on each energy space. This definition selects the nonnegative integral level branch; it does not assert that every positive-energy unitary representation has integral level. The module is **irreducible** if it has no nonzero proper subspace invariant under all current modes.

Define the energy operator on the graded space by $E|_{H_r}=r\operatorname{id}$. The stated mode shift gives $[E,X(n)]=-nX(n)$. This is the convention corresponding to $E=-d$ when adjoining the degree derivation $d$ of [[def-degree-derivation-and-full-untwisted-affine-algebra]], which satisfies $[d,x_n]=n x_n$. The derivation $d$ is not part of the current central extension used in the Sugawara mode formula.

Applying the mode product $u\otimes v\mapsto u(a)v(b)$ shows the corresponding operator identity for every pair of mode indices $a,b$. Thus the diagonal zero-mode action on the inverse tensor vanishes, so $[X(0),S_m]=0$; the indices are unchanged and the normal-ordering split is unchanged. Also $Q$ is positive definite by [F6]–[F7], and finite dimensionality in [F8] gives an orthonormal basis.

$$L_m=-\frac{1}{2(k+h^\vee)}\sum_i\sum_{r\in\mathbb Z}:J_{X_i}(r)J_{X_i}(m-r):.$$
By [[lem-sugawara-quadratic-modes-well-defined]], the mode sum is locally finite on every vector and independent of the chosen dual bases. At the **critical level** $k=-h^\vee$ the scalar denominator is zero and this normalized formula is not defined; no operator is asserted there.

For a finite-dimensional complex simple Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$ as in [[def-loop-algebra-of-a-simple-lie-algebra]], use the invariant form $B$ normalized by long roots of square $2$ in [[def-residue-two-cocycle-on-a-loop-algebra]]. Define the **dual Coxeter number** by $h^\vee=\gamma_B/2$. If a compact real form $\mathfrak k$ from [[def-compact-real-form-of-a-complex-semisimple-lie-algebra]] is additionally supplied, then for every $Q=-B|_{\mathfrak k}$-orthonormal basis $(X_i)$ one has $-\sum_i\operatorname{ad}(X_i)^2=2h^\vee I$. The **untwisted central extension** is the vector space $\overline{L\mathfrak g}=L\mathfrak g\oplus\mathbb Cc$, with $c$ a new nonzero basis vector, and bracket
$$[u+ac,v+bc]=[u,v]_{L\mathfrak g}+\omega(u,v)c.$$
Here $L\mathfrak g$ is [[def-loop-algebra-of-a-simple-lie-algebra]], while $B$ and $\omega$ are exactly the normalized invariant form and residue cocycle of [[def-residue-two-cocycle-on-a-loop-algebra]]. Thus $c$ is central, and for $x_m=x\otimes t^m$,

The bracket is bilinear and alternating by the first cited lemma. Its Jacobi sum has loop component zero by loop Jacobi and central component $\omega([u,v],w)+\omega([v,w],u)+\omega([w,u],v)=0$ by the second lemma. Central inputs give zero directly. Let $\rho$ be a restricted affine-current module of level $k$ as in [[def-positive-energy-affine-module]], and assume $k+h^\vee\ne0$ for the number in [[def-dual-coxeter-number-for-normalized-form]]. Choose any $B$-dual bases $(x_a)$ and $(x^a)$ of $\mathfrak g$. Write $J_x(n)=\rho(x\otimes t^n)$.

For modes, define
$$:J_{x_a}(r)J_{x^a}(s):=\begin{cases}J_{x_a}(r)J_{x^a}(s),&r<0,\\J_{x^a}(s)J_{x_a}(r),&r\ge0.\end{cases}$$
The **Sugawara mode** of index $m\in\mathbb Z$ is
$$L_m=\frac{1}{2(k+h^\vee)}\sum_a\sum_{r\in\mathbb Z}:J_{x_a}(r)J_{x^a}(m-r):.$$
For the compact real form of [[def-compact-real-form-of-a-complex-semisimple-lie-algebra]], put $Q=-B|_{\mathfrak k}$; it is positive by the normalized form in [[def-residue-two-cocycle-on-a-loop-algebra]]. If $(X_i)$ is $Q$-orthonormal, then $( -X_i)$ is its $B$-dual, so the same formula reads
$$L_m=-\frac{1}{2(k+h^\vee)}\sum_i\sum_{r\in\mathbb Z}:J_{X_i}(r)J_{X_i}(m-r):.$$
By [[lem-sugawara-quadratic-modes-well-defined]], the mode sum is locally finite on every vector and independent of the chosen dual bases. At the **critical level** $k=-h^\vee$ the scalar denominator is zero and this normalized formula is not defined; no operator is asserted there.

Let $V$ be a restricted affine-current module of any complex level $k\ne-h^\vee$ as in [[def-positive-energy-affine-module]]. For the modes of [[def-sugawara-modes]], every $x\in\mathfrak g$ and $m,n\in\mathbb Z$ satisfy
$$[L_m,J_x(n)]=-nJ_x(m+n).$$
In particular this holds on all positive-energy unitary modules in the previously considered nonnegative integral level branch.

The **untwisted central extension** is the vector space $\overline{L\mathfrak g}=L\mathfrak g\oplus\mathbb Cc$, with $c$ a new nonzero basis vector, and bracket
$$[u+ac,v+bc]=[u,v]_{L\mathfrak g}+\omega(u,v)c.$$
Here $L\mathfrak g$ is [[def-loop-algebra-of-a-simple-lie-algebra]], while $B$ and $\omega$ are exactly the normalized invariant form and residue cocycle of [[def-residue-two-cocycle-on-a-loop-algebra]]. Their alternatingness and cocycle identity are proved in [[lem-the-loop-residue-form-is-alternating]] and [[lem-the-loop-residue-form-satisfies-the-lie-two-cocycle-identity]]. Thus $c$ is central, and for $x_m=x\otimes t^m$,
$$[x_m,y_n]=[x,y]_{m+n}+m\delta_{m,-n}B(x,y)c.$$
The bracket is bilinear and alternating by the first cited lemma. Its Jacobi sum has loop component zero by loop Jacobi and central component $\omega([u,v],w)+\omega([v,w],u)+\omega([w,u],v)=0$ by the second lemma. Central inputs give zero directly. Hence this defines a Lie algebra. The projection to $L\mathfrak g$ is a surjective Lie homomorphism with kernel $\mathbb Cc$. The vector-space inclusion of the loop algebra need not preserve its bracket. No universal property of this extension is asserted.

Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional complex simple Lie algebra with the invariant form used in [[def-untwisted-affine-central-extension]]. A representation $\rho$ of the loop central extension $\overline{L\mathfrak g}$ is a **restricted affine-current module of level $k\in\mathbb C$** if the central generator acts as $k\operatorname{id}$ and, for every vector $v$ and current $x\in\mathfrak g$, there is an integer $N(v,x)$ such that $\rho(x\otimes t^n)v=0$ for all $n\ge N(v,x)$.

The algebra in this definition is the central extension only; it does not contain the degree derivation. Restrictedness is a mode-truncation condition and does not itself supply an energy grading. A compatible positive-energy grading is extra structure on this current algebra.

The **Virasoro algebra** is the vector space $W\oplus\mathbb C C$, with $W$ from [[def-witt-algebra]] and $C$ a central basis vector, and bracket
$$[L_m,L_n]=(m-n)L_{m+n}+\frac{1}{12}(m^3-m)\delta_{m+n,0}C,$$
where $L_m$ denotes the lift of $d_m$. The bracket with $C$ is zero. The cocycle identity and alternatingness proved in [[lem-witt-cubic-cocycle-is-a-2-cocycle]] make this central extension a Lie algebra. In a representation, the scalar by which $C$ acts is called the **central charge** $c$; the displayed relation then has $c$ in place of $C$.

derivations.claim: Choose a $B$-orthonormal basis $(e_a)$ and abbreviate $a_r=J_{e_a}(r)$. Existence follows by finite diagonalization of the nondegenerate symmetric complex form, rescaling each nonzero diagonal entry by a complex square root. Put $p=m+n$ and let $N_r(A,B)$ mean $AB$ for $r<0$ and $BA$ for $r\ge0$; this subscript specifies the split, not an intrinsic index of $A$. Expanding by [F2] gives $$2q[L_m,L_n]=\sum_{a,r}\bigl(-rN_r(a_{m+r},a_{n-r})-(n-r)N_r(a_r,a_{p-r})\bigr).$$ This equality is algebraic on each $v\in V$. Truncate the original quadratic sum at $|r|\le R$; it stabilizes on $v$ and $L_mv$ by [F1], so its commutator stabilizes to the left side. On the right, in the positive tail the rightmost indices are $r$ or $m+r$, and in the negative tail they are $n-r$ or $p-r$; [F4] kills all these tails for large $R$. Thus the displayed sum is locally finite on $v$, and fixed reindexings below do not create limiting errors.

Reindex the first term by $s=m+r$. It becomes $(m-s)N_{s-m}(a_s,a_{p-s})$, whereas the desired normal order is $N_s$. The second term already has the latter order. Their normally ordered coefficients combine to $(m-s)-(n-s)=m-n$. The order difference in the first term is $$N_{s-m}(a_s,a_{p-s})-N_s(a_s,a_{p-s})=f_m(s)[a_s,a_{p-s}],\qquad f_m(s)=\mathbf1_{s<m}-\mathbf1_{s<0}.$$ For $m>0$ it is the commutator for $0\le s<m$; for $m<0$ it is its negative for $m\le s<0$; for $m=0$ it is zero. Therefore $$2q[L_m,L_n]=2q(m-n)L_p+\sum_s(m-s)f_m(s)\sum_a[a_s,a_{p-s}].$$ Every correction sum is finite, including all zero-index endpoints.

By [F3], $[a_s,a_{p-s}]=sk\delta_{p,0}I_V$, since $[e_a,e_a]=0$ and $B(e_a,e_a)=1$. The correction in step 2.1 is consequently $k\dim(\mathfrak g)\delta_{p,0}I_V$ times $\sum_s s(m-s)f_m(s)$. For $m>0$, the finite sum is $m\sum_{s=0}^{m-1}s-\sum_{s=0}^{m-1}s^2=(m^3-m)/6$. For $m=-u<0$, put $s=-t$ in the negative interval; it becomes $-\sum_{t=1}^{u}t(u-t)=-(u^3-u)/6=(m^3-m)/6$. At $m=0$ both sides vanish. These finite arithmetic identities follow by induction from $\sum_{s=0}^{d-1}s=d(d-1)/2$ and $\sum_{s=0}^{d-1}s^2=d(d-1)(2d-1)/6$. Dividing step 2.1 by $2q\ne0$ gives exactly the stated central charge. The resulting brackets and the scalar central action satisfy [F5], hence give the claimed Virasoro representation, including when $V=0$.

derivations.claim: The $B$-dual basis to $(h,e,f)$ is $(h/2,f,e)$, so $\Omega_B=h^2/2+ef+fe$. In the adjoint representation, $\operatorname{ad}(\Omega_B)e=\frac12[h,[h,e]]+[e,[f,e]]+[f,[e,e]]=2e+2e+0=4e$. By [F2] the operator is the scalar $\gamma_B I$, so its eigenvalue on $e$ is $\gamma_B=4$; [F1] then gives $h^\vee=\gamma_B/2=2$.

At $k=-2$, the denominator in [F3] is $2(k+h^\vee)=2(-2+2)=0$. Division by zero is undefined in $\mathbb C$, so the displayed normalized operator formula does not define $L_m$ at this level. This refutes the statement; it does not assert that every possible renormalized critical-level construction is impossible.

Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional complex simple Lie algebra as in [[def-loop-algebra-of-a-simple-lie-algebra]], with normalized invariant form $B$ from [[def-untwisted-affine-central-extension]]. Let $\rho$ be a restricted affine-current module of level $k$ as in [[def-positive-energy-affine-module]], and assume $k+h^\vee\ne0$ for the number in [[def-dual-coxeter-number-for-normalized-form]]. Choose any $B$-dual bases $(x_a)$ and $(x^a)$ of $\mathfrak g$. Write $J_x(n)=\rho(x\otimes t^n)$.

For modes, define
$$:J_{x_a}(r)J_{x^a}(s):=\begin{cases}J_{x_a}(r)J_{x^a}(s),&r<0,\\J_{x^a}(s)J_{x_a}(r),&r\ge0.\end{cases}$$
The **Sugawara mode** of index $m\in\mathbb Z$ is
$$L_m=\frac{1}{2(k+h^\vee)}\sum_a\sum_{r\in\mathbb Z}:J_{x_a}(r)J_{x^a}(m-r):.$$
For the compact real form of [[def-compact-real-form-of-a-complex-semisimple-lie-algebra]], put $Q=-B|_{\mathfrak k}$; it is positive by the normalized form in [[def-residue-two-cocycle-on-a-loop-algebra]]. If $(X_i)$ is $Q$-orthonormal, then $( -X_i)$ is its $B$-dual, so the same formula reads
$$L_m=-\frac{1}{2(k+h^\vee)}\sum_i\sum_{r\in\mathbb Z}:J_{X_i}(r)J_{X_i}(m-r):.$$
By [[lem-sugawara-quadratic-modes-well-defined]], the mode sum is locally finite on every vector and independent of the chosen dual bases. At the **critical level** $k=-h^\vee$ the scalar denominator is zero and this normalized formula is not defined; no operator is asserted there.

The **untwisted central extension** is the vector space $\overline{L\mathfrak g}=L\mathfrak g\oplus\mathbb Cc$, with $c$ a new nonzero basis vector, and bracket
$$[u+ac,v+bc]=[u,v]_{L\mathfrak g}+\omega(u,v)c.$$
Here $L\mathfrak g$ is [[def-loop-algebra-of-a-simple-lie-algebra]], while $B$ and $\omega$ are exactly the normalized invariant form and residue cocycle of [[def-residue-two-cocycle-on-a-loop-algebra]]. Their alternatingness and cocycle identity are proved in [[lem-the-loop-residue-form-is-alternating]] and [[lem-the-loop-residue-form-satisfies-the-lie-two-cocycle-identity]]. Thus $c$ is central, and for $x_m=x\otimes t^m$,
$$[x_m,y_n]=[x,y]_{m+n}+m\delta_{m,-n}B(x,y)c.$$
The bracket is bilinear and alternating by the first cited lemma. Its Jacobi sum has loop component zero by loop Jacobi and central component $\omega([u,v],w)+\omega([v,w],u)+\omega([w,u],v)=0$ by the second lemma. Central inputs give zero directly. Hence this defines a Lie algebra. The projection to $L\mathfrak g$ is a surjective Lie homomorphism with kernel $\mathbb Cc$. The vector-space inclusion of the loop algebra need not preserve its bracket. No universal property of this extension is asserted.

For a finite-dimensional complex simple Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$ as in [[def-loop-algebra-of-a-simple-lie-algebra]], use the invariant form $B$ normalized by long roots of square $2$ in [[def-residue-two-cocycle-on-a-loop-algebra]]. By [[lem-adjoint-casimir-is-positive-scalar]], the Casimir $\Omega_B$ from [[def-casimir-operator-relative-to-an-invariant-form]] acts in the adjoint representation as $\gamma_B I$ for a unique positive real scalar $\gamma_B$. Define the **dual Coxeter number** by $h^\vee=\gamma_B/2$. Thus, for a $Q=-B|_{\mathfrak k}$-orthonormal basis of a compact real form from [[def-compact-real-form-of-a-complex-semisimple-lie-algebra]], $-\sum_i\operatorname{ad}(X_i)^2=2h^\vee I$; this is the normalization used in the affine central term and every Sugawara denominator below.

Use [[def-loop-algebra-of-a-simple-lie-algebra]]. Fix the positive-real rescaling $B$ of the Killing form whose induced form on the real finite-root span makes every long root have square $2$. The Killing form is nondegenerate, invariant and symmetric by [[lem-finite-lie-engel-trace-criterion-and-killing-nondegeneracy]], and its restriction gives a positive definite real root form by [[lem-finite-semisimple-cartan-root-and-string-structure]], so this rescaling exists. In particular $B([x,y],z)=B(x,[y,z])$.

For $f=\sum_m a_mt^m$ put $f'=\sum_m ma_mt^{m-1}$ and $\operatorname{Res}(f\,dt)=a_{-1}$. Define the residue bilinear form by
$$\omega(x\otimes f,y\otimes q)=B(x,y)\operatorname{Res}(f'q\,dt).$$
The formula is balanced and complex bilinear, so extends uniquely to the tensor product. In particular,
$$\omega(x_m,y_n)=m\delta_{m,-n}B(x,y).$$
The Kronecker symbol is one when $m=-n$ and zero otherwise. This form is in fact an alternating Lie-algebra two-cocycle. For Laurent polynomials $f,q$, the residue of $(fq)'$ is zero, so $\operatorname{Res}(f'q\,dt)=-\operatorname{Res}(fq'\,dt)$; symmetry of $B$ gives skew-symmetry, and in characteristic zero also $\omega(a,a)=0$. For pure tensors $x\otimes f,y\otimes q,z\otimes h$, invariance and symmetry of $B$ make the three factors $B([x,y],z)$, $B([y,z],x)$, and $B([z,x],y)$ equal. The cyclic cocycle sum is therefore that common factor times
$$\operatorname{Res}\bigl(((fq)'h+(qh)'f+(hf)'q)\,dt\bigr)=2\operatorname{Res}((fqh)'\,dt)=0.$$
Trilinearity extends the identity to all loop-algebra elements. Thus the terminology “two-cocycle” records a proved property of the defined form, not merely an intended later use.

For any long root $\alpha$, opposite root vectors normalized by $[e_\alpha,f_\alpha]=\alpha^\vee$ satisfy
$$B(e_\alpha,f_\alpha)=\frac{2}{(\alpha,\alpha)}=1.$$
The equality follows by pairing $[e_\alpha,f_\alpha]$ with the Cartan and using invariance. A later result identifies the highest root and proves that it is long; no highest-root existence claim is used here.

Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional complex simple Lie algebra with the invariant form used in [[def-untwisted-affine-central-extension]]. A representation $\rho$ of the loop central extension $\overline{L\mathfrak g}$ is a **restricted affine-current module of level $k\in\mathbb C$** if the central generator acts as $k\operatorname{id}$ and, for every vector $v$ and current $x\in\mathfrak g$, there is an integer $N(v,x)$ such that $\rho(x\otimes t^n)v=0$ for all $n\ge N(v,x)$.

The algebra in this definition is the central extension only; it does not contain the degree derivation. Restrictedness is a mode-truncation condition and does not itself supply an energy grading. A compatible positive-energy grading is extra structure on this current algebra.

derivations.claim: Choose a $B$-orthonormal complex basis $(e_a)$. Such a basis exists by finite-dimensional diagonalization: a nonzero symmetric nondegenerate form has a vector of nonzero square (otherwise polarization makes it zero), rescale that vector using a square root in $\mathbb C$, and induct on its nondegenerate orthogonal complement. Invariance gives $\sum_a([x,e_a]\otimes e_a+e_a\otimes[x,e_a])=0$: in this basis the matrix of $\operatorname{ad}(x)$ is skew-symmetric, since $B([x,u],v)=-B(u,[x,v])$. Also $\sum_a[e_a,[e_a,x]]=2h^\vee x$ by [F3]. This choice concerns only $\mathfrak g$, not an inner product on $V$.

Fix $v\in V$ and integers $m,n$. Expand $[J_x(n),T_m]$ by the product rule in the original normal order. All terms are finite on $v$: for $r\to+\infty$ the rightmost current or its commutator has index $r$ or $r+n$, and for $r\to-\infty$ it has index $m-r$ or $m-r+n$. These kill $v$ beyond a common bound, using [F5] for the finite family $e_a,[x,e_a]$. To identify the expansion with the commutator, the original truncated quadratic sum also stabilizes on both $v$ and $J_x(n)v$ by [F1]. Thus a sufficiently large cutoff gives the actual commutator, and all following identities are identities of eventually constant finite sums on $v$. Each factor contributes $nkJ_x(m+n)/2$ from the central term in [F2], by $\sum_aB(x,e_a)e_a=x$; their sum is $nkJ_x(m+n)$. This includes coincident indices: the two product-rule contributions are both retained.

Write $p=m+n$, $A_{\alpha,\beta}=\sum_aJ_{[x,e_a]}(\alpha)J_{e_a}(\beta)$ and $D_{\alpha,\beta}=\sum_aJ_{e_a}(\alpha)J_{[x,e_a]}(\beta)$ for $\alpha+\beta=p$. The noncentral expansion in step 2.1 is $\sum_{\alpha+\beta=p}(a_{\alpha,\beta}A_{\alpha,\beta}+b_{\alpha,\beta}D_{\alpha,\beta})$, with $$a_{\alpha,\beta}=\tfrac12(\mathbf1_{\alpha<n}+\mathbf1_{\beta\ge0}),\qquad b_{\alpha,\beta}=\tfrac12(\mathbf1_{\alpha<0}+\mathbf1_{\beta\ge n}).$$ Indeed the first normal-order half $r<0$ contributes $A$ at $\alpha=r+n<n$ and $D$ at $\alpha=r<0$; the reversed half $r\ge0$ contributes $A$ at $\beta=r\ge0$ and $D$ at $\beta=r+n\ge n$. The invariant tensor of step 1.1 gives $D_{\alpha,\beta}=-A_{\alpha,\beta}$. Set $f_n(j)=\mathbf1_{j<n}-\mathbf1_{j<0}$. Then $a-b=(f_n(\alpha)+f_n(\beta))/2$. Cancellation leaves a finite sum, since $f_n$ is supported on $0\le j<n$ for $n>0$, on $n\le j<0$ with value $-1$ for $n<0$, and is zero for $n=0$. The uncancelled tails before this cancellation are legitimate too: for $\alpha$ sufficiently negative the rightmost index $\beta$ is sufficiently positive, and for $\alpha$ sufficiently positive both coefficients are zero.

Exchange $\alpha,\beta$ in the term with coefficient $f_n(\beta)$. By the same invariant tensor, $A_{\beta,\alpha}=-\sum_aJ_{e_a}(\beta)J_{[x,e_a]}(\alpha)$. Hence the noncentral part is $$\frac12\sum_{\alpha+\beta=p}f_n(\alpha)\sum_a[J_{[x,e_a]}(\alpha),J_{e_a}(\beta)].$$ Here $B([x,e_a],e_a)=B(x,[e_a,e_a])=0$, so there is no additional central term. Moreover $\sum_a\bigl[\,[x,e_a],e_a\bigr]=\sum_a[e_a,[e_a,x]]=2h^\vee x$. As $\sum_{\alpha\in\mathbb Z}f_n(\alpha)=n$, including $n=0$ and negative $n$, [F2] reduces the displayed finite sum to $nh^\vee J_x(p)$. Together with step 2.1, this gives $[J_x(n),T_m]=n(k+h^\vee)J_x(p)$. Divide by $q\ne0$ and reverse the commutator to obtain the claim.
